                                           PROJECT NO. 58481


 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT LARGE                        §         PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LOAD INTERCONNECTION                                                    OF TEXAS
                                                      §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA


                    TEXAS PUBLIC POWER ASSOCIATION’S RESPONSE TO
                              QUESTIONS FOR COMMENT

       The Texas Public Power Association (TPPA) appreciates the opportunity to respond to the
questions for comment issued by the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission) related to
rulemaking to implement large load interconnection standards under Public Utility Regulatory Act
(PURA). These comments are submitted on behalf of TPPA and do not necessarily reflect the opinions of
any individual TPPA member.

       Formed in 1978, TPPA is the statewide association for the 72 municipally owned utilities (MOUs)
in Texas. TPPA membership also includes several electric cooperatives and joint action agencies, as well
as the Lower Colorado River Authority. TPPA members serve urban, suburban, and rural Texas and vary
in size from large, vertically-integrated utilities to relatively small distribution-only systems. We are proud
to serve approximately 5.1 million Texans across the state. Most of our members operate within the
Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) region, though several are located within either the
Southwest Power Pool (SPP) or Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) region. MOUs offer
a long track record of stability, and we serve an essential role in providing secure and reliable power to
the wholesale electricity markets in these regions, including ERCOT. Many of our member systems have
been providing stable and reliable electric service to communities in Texas for over 100 years, and
collectively, our members provide more than 13,000 MW of generation and maintain more than 8,500
miles of high-voltage transmission assets or more than 15% of the transmission in ERCOT.

       On December 1, 2025, the Commission issued a discussion draft, seeking comments by December
19, 2025. These responses are timely filed.



                               I.      Responses to Commission Questions
1. Should the commission define parameters for determining whether a large load customer is
   pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request? If so, how should the commission
   define those parameters?
   TPPA Comments                                                                             Page 1 of 12
         TPPA supports the Commission’s discussion draft and its language stating that a “substantially
similar” interconnection request is one in which approval of one project would cause a customer to
materially change, delay, or withdraw another interconnection request. TPPA believes this description
adequately communicates the intent of reporting “substantially similar” projects, where the outcome of
one request directly affects the parameters or timing of another.

        TPPA is concerned that large load customers may choose to withhold information by invoking
protections for competitively sensitive data with the interconnecting electric utility. TPPA recommends
that if it is later discovered that a large load customer failed to report all substantially similar projects, the
interconnecting electric utility should not be held responsible for any information the large load customer
failed to provide.



2. Proposed subsections (c)(3), (e)(3), and (h)(3) require the disclosure of specific information
    related to a substantially similar request for interconnection and allows a large load customer to
    anonymize competitively sensitive details. Should the commission list what is and is not
    competitively sensitive (e.g., load zone is not competitively sensitive information)? If so, what
    information should and should not be considered competitively sensitive such that the
    interconnecting utility and ERCOT can identify whether there is a duplicate request, or a
    request is unlikely to materialize?

        TPPA recommends that the following items be explicitly deemed not competitively sensitive: the
name of the interconnecting electric utility; the contracted peak demand (or the requested peak demand if
the contracted peak demand is unknown); and the requested interconnection date.



3. Should the commission require a large load customer to notify the interconnecting electric utility
    and ERCOT of any change to information that is initially disclosed in response to this rule or
    only material changes to the information disclosed? If only material changes, how should
    “material change” be defined?

        If this question is asking about material changes to information reported under 25.194(c), (e), and
(h), then TPPA believes all information disclosed under these subsections is material and should therefore
require the large load customer to notify the interconnecting electric utility of any change to that
information.

    TPPA Comments                                                                               Page 2 of 12
 4. Proposed subsection (k)(1) authorizes an interconnecting electric utility to refund 20% of a large
    load customer’s security after energization and ratably as the large load customer meets the
    milestones identified in the customer’s schedule for phased energization of its contracted load.
    Should the commission standardize the rate for refund for reaching milestones identified in the
    customer’s schedule for phased energization (e.g., 20% for each year of operations until the full
    amount of security is refunded)? If so, how should the commission standardize the refund?

           TPPA addresses this comment below under Refunding Financial Security.



5. Are changes to the commission’s other substantive rules necessary to align with this rulemaking?
    If so, what changes need to be made to which rules?

           At this time, TPPA is not aware of any Commission rules that conflict with the provisions included
in this discussion draft.



                     II.     Comments and Recommendations on the Discussion Draft

           TPPA commends Commission Staff on the well-developed discussion draft issued for comments.
The draft presents the relevant issues and processes in a clear and understandable manner, and TPPA
applauds Commission Staff’s efforts in preparing it.

Interconnecting Electric Utility and Retail Service Provider

           Proposed 25.194(c) states, “…a large load customer seeking to interconnect in the electric utility’s
retail delivery service area.” TPPA notes that this language assumes the interconnecting electric utility is
operating within its own retail delivery service area. In practice, that assumption can be incorrect.
Frequently, the interconnecting electric utility, acting as the transmission service provider, completes an
interconnection in a retail delivery service area served by a different utility. In those circumstances, the
distribution service provider is the retail service provider for that area, not the interconnecting electric
utility.



Large Load Interconnection Studies

           In proposed 25.194(b)(9), a large load interconnection study is defined as “a set of studies required
in the ERCOT protocols to determine compliance with ERCOT planning requirements and the scope of
    TPPA Comments                                                                              Page 3 of 12
 upgrades to existing facilities or new facilities needed to serve a large load customer requesting
interconnection.” TPPA notes that this term appears to be used inconsistently throughout the rule to
describe studies conducted solely by the interconnecting electric utility and studies conducted by both the
interconnecting electric utility and ERCOT.

       It is TPPA’s understanding that the ERCOT protocols describe the studies ERCOT conducts and
requires for the interconnection of a large load to ensure the reliability and stability of the ERCOT system
as a whole. Many utilities also perform additional studies to ensure the reliability and stability of their
own systems. TPPA does not take a position on whether the defined term should refer only to ERCOT’s
studies, only to the interconnecting electric utility’s studies, or to both. TPPA’s concern is that the term
be used consistently and intentionally throughout the rule.

       For example, if the term “large load interconnection study” is intended to refer only to the
interconnecting electric utility’s studies, it is unclear why the study fee contemplated in proposed
25.194(c)(7) also includes ERCOT’s study costs. Additionally, proposed 25.194(d) contemplates the
interconnecting electric utility providing ERCOT with the results of the interconnection study, which
suggests that ERCOT did not participate in the study.

Finally, TPPA emphasizes the importance of allowing the interconnecting electric utility to retain
flexibility and discretion in determining the studies required for a large load customer’s interconnection
request.



Study Fee

       Proposed 25.194(c)(7) describes a requirement for a large load customer to provide the
interconnecting electric utility and ERCOT with payment for conducting the large load interconnection
study. TPPA strongly supports the flexibility provided within this provision, which ensures that if the
costs of the studies exceed the threshold established in the proposed rule, the large load customer is still
required to pay the actual costs of the studies.

       However, as noted above, it is unclear to TPPA which studies are encompassed by the term “large
load interconnection study” and who is responsible for completing them. If the term does include studies
to be completed by ERCOT, TPPA requests clarification on the process for conveying the amount owed
by the large load customer to ERCOT.



   TPPA Comments                                                                           Page 4 of 12
 Discretionary Service Agreement and Intermediate Agreement

       TPPA notes that the only actions contemplated between the execution of a discretionary service
agreement and an intermediate agreement appear to be the submission of the large load interconnection
study to ERCOT, after which ERCOT may require additional studies, and an update to the disclosures. As
noted above under Large Load Interconnection Studies, the term “large load interconnection study” is
ambiguous as to whether it refers to studies conducted by and for the interconnecting electric utility, or
also by and for ERCOT.

       As currently proposed, TPPA questions the necessity of requiring both a discretionary service
agreement and an intermediate agreement, since very little substantive action occurs between the two. As
an alternative, the Commission could require the discretionary service agreement, along with the
associated disclosures, study fee, and $50,000 per MW security, to be provided prior to the electric utility
initiating interconnection studies. Absent this update, TPPA sees no need for two separate agreements and
believes the process could be simplified by requiring a single agreement that encompasses both (e)(8) and
(h)(8), regardless of whether the payments are due simultaneously or on a defined schedule.

       Finally, TPPA requests clarification of whether the proposed intermediate agreement serves as the
interconnection agreement governing the level of service and terms of service for the large load customer.
If the intermediate agreement does not constitute the interconnection agreement containing these terms,
then TPPA requests that the Commission clarify in the rule when this agreement is to be completed in
relation to the interconnection process.



Reporting Co-Located Generation and Backup Generation

       Proposed 25.194(c), (e), and (h) require large load customers to disclose and update information
related to their interconnection requests, including information on potential backup generation. Proposed
25.194(b)(1) defines backup generating facilities as “generation facilities that are not capable of exporting
energy to the ERCOT transmission system and that, in aggregate, can serve at least 50% of on-site
contracted peak demand.” TPPA supports this definition, as it is consistent with PURA § 37.0561(d).

       However, TPPA believes that similar information regarding co-located generation and backup
generation that is capable of exporting to the grid, or that is not planned to serve at least 50% of the
anticipated demand, is equally important in evaluating the interconnection request. Accordingly, TPPA
recommends that proposed subsections (c), (e), and (h) be revised to require large load customers to

   TPPA Comments                                                                            Page 5 of 12
 disclose plans for co-located generation and backup generation that could export to the ERCOT grid or
that would not be able to serve at least 50% of the large load’s requested or contracted peak demand.



Additional Studies

        Proposed 25.194(g) contemplates ERCOT notifying the interconnecting electric utility that a large
load’s interconnection request requires additional studies. Specifically, 25.194(g)(1) notes that ERCOT
will notify the interconnecting electric utility of the reason additional studies are necessary, the type of
additional study required, and an estimated timeline for completing the study.

        It is unclear to TPPA whether the additional studies are to be conducted by the interconnecting
electric utility or by ERCOT. However, if the studies are to be conducted by the interconnecting electric
utility, TPPA objects to ERCOT establishing the timeline for completion. Many interconnecting electric
utilities that are MOUs are already stretched in their ability to complete the required studies for all large
load interconnection requests. While MOUs will seek to complete additional studies as reasonably as
possible, ultimately only the MOU can determine the timeframe for completing these studies.



Financial Security and CIAC

        TPPA supports the proposed rule, which requires a security payment based both on a dollar-per-
MW basis (proposed 25.194(e)(8)) and on the interconnecting electric utility’s costs to procure equipment
to facilitate the large load’s interconnection (proposed 25.194(h)(8)). TPPA believes there is significant
risk that large amounts of transmission facilities will be procured and constructed for large load customers
who ultimately do not fully utilize these facilities. A strong financial security requirement will help deter
this type of behavior.1 TPPA also supports the proposed rule’s position in (h)(9) that the CIAC will cover
the interconnecting electricity utility’s expected costs to interconnect the customer, which TPPA believes
to include the costs associated with procuring and constructing transmission facilities associated with the
large load’s interconnection.




1
 At this time, TPPA does not have a specific opinion regarding whether the proposed (e)(8) $50,000/MW security amount or
the (h)(8) security amount related to the costs of procuring long-lead-time facilities is adequate; however, TPPA emphasizes
the importance of ensuring that financial security effectively sends a strong signal to deter large load customers from
pursuing duplicative or redundant interconnections or underutilizing their requested capacity in order to ensure all other
ratepayers are held harmless.
    TPPA Comments                                                                                        Page 6 of 12
        TPPA recognizes that, under the proposed rule, there may be a perception that a large load
customer is required to remit duplicative payments through the security requirement in subsection (h)(8)
and the CIAC in subsection (h)(9). TPPA believes, however, that the security required under subsection
(h)(8) is not duplicative of the costs covered by the CIAC. While both provisions rely on the same
underlying measurements (costs to procure and construct facilities), they serve distinct purposes. The
CIAC is intended to recover the costs of interconnection, whereas the security required under subsections
(e)(8) or (h)(8) is intended to provide certainty that the interconnection will in fact proceed. This security
is particularly important if the Commission ultimately elects not to adopt proposed subsection (h)(9)(B)
in the final rule, as it would both increase confidence in the viability of the interconnection and potentially
offset costs associated with system upgrades. However, if TPPA’s understanding of the respective
purposes of the security proposed under paragraph (h)(8) and the CIAC proposed under paragraph (h)(9)
is incorrect, TPPA requests clarification regarding the distinction between these two payments and the
specific costs intended to be covered by each. Finally, if certain costs are intended to be recovered solely
through subsection (h)(8), TPPA requests that the rule provide clear certainty that such security is not
refundable and is instead to be applied toward those procurement and construction costs.



System Upgrades

       As noted in proposed 25.194(h)(9)(B), TPPA understands the Commission’s intent to require large
load customers to pay for “costs associated with system upgrades that would not be required but for the
interconnecting large load customer.” However, TPPA is concerned that this approach may be
discriminatory, as the costs of building a facility would be allocated to a single customer even though the
facility will ultimately be used by the entire system.

       TPPA supports the Commission’s goal of ensuring that large load customers pay their fair share
of costs, but believes this issue is more appropriately addressed under Project No. 58484, which evaluates
transmission cost recovery. Through Project No. 58484, the Commission can develop a transmission cost
allocation methodology that ensures all customers pay a just and equitable share of system-wide costs,
including system upgrade costs.




   TPPA Comments                                                                             Page 7 of 12
 Reassignment of CIAC Payments to the First Mover

         TPPA strongly discourages the Commission from reassigning CIAC given the administrative
complexity, however if the Commission chooses to move forward with assigning system upgrade costs to
the interconnecting large load customer that caused the need for the upgrades, TPPA provides the
following comments on proposed 25.194(h)(9)(C) regarding the reallocation of costs back to the first
mover.

Entity Responsible for Reallocation

         TPPA requests clarity regarding which entity is responsible for calculating, notifying, collecting,
and distributing the CIAC payments as proposed. TPPA believes that if the Commission proceeds with
this reallocation, that the process and refunds will be highly controversial and administratively complex.
To that end, TPPA asserts that this responsibility should not fall to the interconnecting electric utility or
retail service provider, as they already have numerous responsibilities related to maintaining system
reliability, interconnecting new load and generation, and providing service to their customers.

         If the Commission proceeds with the drafted process, TPPA recommends that the Commission
itself be the entity responsible for calculating the costs to be reassigned, notifying the large load customers
of the reassignment, and collecting and redistributing the funds.

         If, instead, the Commission proposes that the interconnecting electric utility or the retail service
provider assume these responsibilities, TPPA requests that the rule codify the full process, including:

         •   A formula for calculating the costs to be reassigned;2
         •   The method for notification and associated timelines for responding and remitting payment;
         •   The type of payment acceptable to the interconnecting electric utility or retail service provider;
             and
         •   The method for remitting payments to the appropriate parties.

Clarification of Terms

TPPA seeks clarification on key terms to reduce ambiguity and potential disputes:


2
  The written description of the formula provided in the proposed rule presents several concerns. First, it includes undefined
terms that could be subject to dispute. Second, it contains vague language describing specific calculations, such as the term
“fraction.” Third, it does not account for the complexity of the calculation, which may need to be applied multiple times to
multiple parties as additional large loads connect and utilize the facilities. TPPA believes that including a clearly defined
formula in the rule would better ensure that the calculation is performed accurately and consistently.


    TPPA Comments                                                                                           Page 8 of 12
        •    “Original CIAC,” which could include more than one large load customer’s CIAC and may
            include costs exceeding those associated with the transmission asset the new large load
            customer is interconnecting to;
       •    “Remaining net book value” and “book value,” as the calculation of these amounts could be
            contested depending on the party performing the calculation. If the intent is for the electric
            utility to perform these calculations, TPPA requests that the rule expressly specify that the
            applicable book values are to be determined based on the electric utility’s calculations; and
       •    “CIAC payments,” which in this proposed rule refers to credits provided back to the original
            large load customer, whereas currently it refers to payments made by the original and any new
            large load customer to the interconnecting electric utility for the development of the
            interconnection.

Applicability to Other Customers

       TPPA notes that the proposed rule does not recognize that generation facilities and loads not
classified as large loads customers under this rule may also interconnect to the new facilities. TPPA
understands that these non-large load customers would not be required to pay CIAC payments to the
original large load customer under this proposal; only new large load customers would be subject to such
payments.

Timing Limitations

       Finally, TPPA recommends that the rule clearly state that this provision applies only to facilities
built after the adoption of the rule, and that the reallocation process ceases for facilities that have been
energized for more than five years.



Forms of Payment for CIAC

       Proposed §25.194(h)(9)(D) provides that a large load may remit CIAC payments to an electric
utility in the form of cash, a corporate or parental guaranty, or a letter of credit. While TPPA does not at
this time object to these instruments being acceptable forms of payment for security deposits, TPPA
recognizes that both guaranties and letters of credit are impractical for CIAC payments. CIAC funds are
intended to be applied directly and expeditiously to the construction of interconnection facilities.
Requiring an electric utility to draw upon a letter of credit or pursue payment under a guaranty would



   TPPA Comments                                                                           Page 9 of 12
 introduce administrative delays and could hinder timely construction. Accordingly, TPPA recommends
that cash be the sole acceptable form of payment for CIAC obligations.



Refunding Financial Security

       As TPPA reads proposed 25.194(k)(1), the interconnecting utility is required to refund 20% of the
remaining security when the large load customer energizes. Additional security refunds are provided as
the large load customer meets milestones on its ramp schedule, proportional to the amount of load yet to
be energized to reach its contracted peak demand. However, proposed 25.194(k)(2) provides that any
remaining security balance must be refunded once the large load customer has sustained operations at its
contracted peak demand for five years. TPPA notes that there is a direct conflict between 25.194(k)(1)
and 25.194(k)(2), because under (k)(1) the total security will already have been refunded once the large
load reaches its contracted peak demand, leaving no security to be refunded under (k)(2).

       TPPA supports the concept in 25.194(k)(2), whereby the large load customer only receives a
complete refund of its security if it sustains operations at its contracted peak demand for a specified period,
and recommends extending that period to 10 years. To ensure security remains available for distribution
after this period, TPPA recommends refining 25.194(k)(1) so that only 50% of the remaining security is
returned ratably as the large load meets its ramp schedule milestones.

       Additionally, as noted above, TPPA seeks clarification that the security refund contemplated under
subsection (k) applies to security provided under both proposed subsections (e)(8) and (h)(8), and that the
security provided under subsection (h)(8) is not intended to cover an electric utility’s costs for procuring
equipment and services to facilitate the interconnection, as those costs are addressed through and paid
under the CIAC.



Additional Standards Established by MOUs and Electric Cooperatives

       PURA § 37.0561(l) provides, “The commission may not limit the authority of a municipally owned
utility or an electric cooperative to impose electric service requirements for large load customers on their
systems in addition to the standards adopted under this section.” The proposed rule does not appear to
contemplate that a MOU or electric cooperative may develop additional standards necessary for their
system. TPPA recommends that the exact language of PURA § 37.0561(l) be added as a new subsection
in the rule to ensure consistency and maintain conformity between the Commission rule and PURA.

   TPPA Comments                                                                            Page 10 of 12
                                         III.   Conclusion

       At this time, TPPA has no additional comments on the questions for comment.

       TPPA appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments. As always, TPPA looks forward to
working with the Commission, Commission Staff, and stakeholders on this important discussion in the
coming months.




Dated: December 19, 2025
                                          Respectfully,

                                          ____________________
                                          Mariah Benson
                                          Regulatory Affairs Manager
                                          Texas Public Power Association
                                          PO Box 82768
                                          Austin, Texas 78708
                                          (512) 472-5965
                                          mbenson@tppa.com




   TPPA Comments                                                                     Page 11 of 12
                    Texas Public Power Association’s (TPPA) Executive Summary

•   TPPA recommends that an interconnecting electric utility not be held responsible for information
    large load customers fail to provide.
•   TPPA recommends that the following items be explicitly deemed not competitively sensitive: the
    name of the interconnecting electric utility; the contracted peak demand, or the requested peak
    demand if the contracted peak demand is unknown; and the requested interconnection date.
•   TPPA recommends the rule recognize that the interconnecting electric utility will not always also be
    the retail service provider.
•   TPPA requests that the rule clarify whether large load interconnection studies are to be conducted by
    the interconnecting electric utility, ERCOT, or both. If the studies include ERCOT’s analyses, TPPA
    recommends that the rule provide additional information regarding the calculation of the study fee
    for ERCOT’s costs versus the interconnecting electric utility’s costs.
•   TPPA recommends that the Commission provide clarification on when the interconnection
    agreement should be issued and the information it should contain.
•   TPPA recommends that the discretionary service agreement, including the $50,000 per MW security,
    be required before the interconnecting electric utility initiates any studies.
•   TPPA recommends large load customers be required to disclose plans for co-located generation and
    backup generation that could export to the ERCOT grid or that would be unable to serve at least 50%
    of the large load’s requested or contracted peak demand.
•   TPPA recommends that the rule clarify whether additional studies requested by ERCOT will be
    completed by the interconnecting electric utility or by ERCOT. If the additional studies are to be
    completed by the interconnecting electric utility, TPPA objects to ERCOT determining the timeline
    for completion of those studies.
•   TPPA supports the Commission requiring two securities—the $50,000 per MW security and an
    amount aligned with the costs to interconnect the large load customer—to be held until after the
    large load customer has completed and energized its interconnection. TPPA believes that the high
    security requirements will ensure that large load customers pursue interconnection requests
    intentionally and provide the market with certainty regarding realistic load interconnection requests.
•   TPPA recommends that the rule not specify that large load customers will fund system upgrade costs
    incurred by the interconnecting electric utility to complete their interconnection.
•   TPPA strongly recommends the rule not require a CIAC reallocation from new large load customers
    to original large load customers. However, if the Commission proceeds with this approach, TPPA
    requests clarification on how CIAC payments will be calculated, who will calculate them, and the
    processes for notification, collection, and distribution. TPPA asserts that this responsibility should
    not fall on the interconnecting electric utility or retail service provider.
•   TPPA recommends that cash be the sole acceptable form of payment for CIAC obligations.
•   TPPA recommends that the rule extend the period during which the interconnecting electric utility
    holds security from five years to ten years. Additionally, TPPA recommends refining § 25.194(k)(1)
    so that only 50% of the remaining security is returned ratably as the large load customer meets its
    ramp schedule milestones.
•   TPPA recommends that the exact language of PURA § 37.0561(l), regarding MOUs’ and electric
    cooperatives’ authority to impose additional electric service requirements, be added as a new
    subsection in the rule to ensure consistency and maintain conformity between the Commission rule
    and PURA.
    TPPA Comments                                                                       Page 12 of 12

                     II.     Comments and Recommendations on the Discussion Draft

           TPPA commends Commission Staff on the well-developed discussion draft issued for comments.
The draft presents the relevant issues and processes in a clear and understandable manner, and TPPA
applauds Commission Staff' s efforts in preparing it.

Interconnecting Electric Utility and Retail Service Provider

           Proposed 25.194(c) states, "...a large load customer seeking to interconnect in the electric utility's
retail delivery service area." TPPA notes that this language assumes the interconnecting electric utility is
operating within its own retail delivery service area. In practice, that assumption can be incorrect.
Frequently, the interconnecting electric utility, acting as the transmission service provider, completes an
interconnection in a retail delivery service area served by a different utility. In those circumstances, the
distribution service provider is the retail service provider for that area, not the interconnecting electric
utility.



Large Load Interconnection Studies

           In proposed 25.194(b)(9), a large load interconnection study is defined as "a set of studies required
in the ERCOT protocols to determine compliance with ERCOT planning requirements and the scope of
    TPPA Comments                                                                               Page 3 of 12
 upgrades to existing facilities or new facilities needed to serve a large load customer requesting
interconnection." TPPA notes that this term appears to be used inconsistently throughout the rule to
describe studies conducted solely by the interconnecting electric utility and studies conducted by both the
interconnecting electric utility and ERCOT.

       It is TPPA' s understanding that the ERCOT protocols describe the studies ERCOT conducts and
requires for the interconnection of a large load to ensure the reliability and stability of the ERCOT system
as a whole. Many utilities also perform additional studies to ensure the reliability and stability of their
own systems. TPPA does not take a position on whether the defined term should refer only to ERCOT's
studies, only to the interconnecting electric utility' s studies, or to both. TPPA' s concern is that the term
be used consistently and intentionally throughout the rule.

       For example, if the term "large load interconnection study" is intended to refer only to the
interconnecting electric utility's studies, it is unclear why the study fee contemplated in proposed
25.194(c)(7) also includes ERCOT' s study costs. Additionally, proposed 25. 194(d) contemplates the
interconnecting electric utility providing ERCOT with the results of the interconnection study, which
suggests that ERCOT did not participate in the study.

Finally, TPPA emphasizes the importance of allowing the interconnecting electric utility to retain
flexibility and discretion in determining the studies required for a large load customer's interconnection
request.



Study Fee

       Proposed 25.194(c)(7) describes a requirement for a large load customer to provide the
interconnecting electric utility and ERCOT with payment for conducting the large load interconnection
study. TPPA strongly supports the flexibility provided within this provision, which ensures that if the
costs of the studies exceed the threshold established in the proposed rule, the large load customer is still
required to pay the actual costs of the studies.

       However, as noted above, it is unclear to TPPA which studies are encompassed by the term "large
load interconnection study" and who is responsible for completing them. If the term does include studies
to be completed by ERCOT, TPPA requests clarification on the process for conveying the amount owed
by the large load customer to ERCOT.

 Discretionary Service Agreement and Intermediate Agreement

       TPPA notes that the only actions contemplated between the execution of a discretionary service
agreement and an intermediate agreement appear to be the submission of the large load interconnection
study to ERCOT, after which ERCOT may require additional studies, and an update to the disclosures. As
noted above under Large Load Interconnection Studies, the term "large load interconnection study" is
ambiguous as to whether it refers to studies conducted by and for the interconnecting electric utility, or
also by and for ERCOT.

       As currently proposed, TPPA questions the necessity of requiring both a discretionary service
agreement and an intermediate agreement, since very little substantive action occurs between the two. As
an alternative, the Commission could require the discretionary service agreement, along with the
associated disclosures, study fee, and $50,000 per MW security, to be provided prior to the electric utility
initiating interconnection studies. Absent this update, TPPA sees no need for two separate agreements and
believes the process could be simplified by requiring a single agreement that encompasses both (e)(8) and
(h)(8), regardless of whether the payments are due simultaneously or on a defined schedule.

       Finally, TPPA requests clarification of whether the proposed intermediate agreement serves as the
interconnection agreement governing the level of service and terms of service for the large load customer.
If the intermediate agreement does not constitute the interconnection agreement containing these terms,
then TPPA requests that the Commission clarify in the rule when this agreement is to be completed in
relation to the interconnection process.



Reporting Co-Located Generation and Backup Generation

       Proposed 25.194(c), (e), and (h) require large load customers to disclose and update information
related to their interconnection requests, including information on potential backup generation. Proposed
25.194(b)(1) defines backup generating facilities as "generation facilities that are not capable of exporting
energy to the ERCOT transmission system and that, in aggregate, can serve at least 50% of on-site
contracted peak demand." TPPA supports this definition, as it is consistent with PURA § 37.0561(d)

       However, TPPA believes that similar information regarding co-located generation and backup
generation that is capable of exporting to the grid, or that is not planned to serve at least 50% of the
anticipated demand, is equally important in evaluating the interconnection request. Accordingly, TPPA
recommends that proposed subsections (c), (e), and (h) be revised to require large load customers to

Additional Studies

         Proposed 25. 194(g) contemplates ERCOT notifying the interconnecting electric utility that a large
load's interconnection request requires additional studies. Specifically, 25.194(g)(1) notes that ERCOT
will notify the interconnecting electric utility of the reason additional studies are necessary, the type of
additional study required, and an estimated timeline for completing the study.

         It is unclear to TPPA whether the additional studies are to be conducted by the interconnecting
electric utility or by ERCOT. However, if the studies are to be conducted by the interconnecting electric
utility, TPPA objects to ERCOT establishing the timeline for completion. Many interconnecting electric
utilities that are MOUs are already stretched in their ability to complete the required studies for all large
load interconnection requests. While MOUs will seek to complete additional studies as reasonably as
possible, ultimately only the MOU can determine the timeframe for completing these studies.



Financial Security and CIAC

         TPPA supports the proposed rule, which requires a security payment based both on a dollar-per-
MW basis (proposed 25.194(e)(8)) and on the interconnecting electric utility' s costs to procure equipment
to facilitate the large load' s interconnection (proposed 25.194(h)(8)). TPPA believes there is significant
risk that large amounts oftransmission facilities will be procured and constructed for large load customers
who ultimately do not fully utilize these facilities. A strong financial security requirement will help deter
this type of behavior. l TPPA also supports the proposed rule' s position in (h)(9) that the CIAC will cover
the interconnecting electricity utility' s expected costs to interconnect the customer, which TPPA believes
to include the costs associated with procuring and constructing transmission facilities associated with the
large load' s interconnection.

        TPPA recognizes that, under the proposed rule, there may be a perception that a large load
customer is required to remit duplicative payments through the security requirement in subsection (h)(8)
and the CIAC in subsection (h)(9). TPPA believes, however, that the security required under subsection
(h)(8) is not duplicative of the costs covered by the CIAC. While both provisions rely on the same
underlying measurements (costs to procure and construct facilities), they serve distinct purposes. The
CIAC is intended to recover the costs of interconnection, whereas the security required under subsections
(e)(8) or (h)(8) is intended to provide certainty that the interconnection will in fact proceed. This security
is particularly important if the Commission ultimately elects not to adopt proposed subsection (h)(9)(B)
in the final rule, as it would both increase confidence in the viability ofthe interconnection andpotentially
offset costs associated with system upgrades. However, if TPPA's understanding of the respective
purposes of the security proposed under paragraph (h)(8) and the CIAC proposed under paragraph (h)(9)
is incorrect, TPPA requests clarification regarding the distinction between these two payments and the
specific costs intended to be covered by each. Finally, if certain costs are intended to be recovered solely
through subsection (h)(8), TPPA requests that the rule provide clear certainty that such security is not
refundable and is instead to be applied toward those procurement and construction costs.



System Upgrades

       As noted in proposed 25.194(h)(9)(B), TPPA understands the Commission' s intent to require large
load customers to pay for "costs associated with system upgrades that would not be required but for the
interconnecting large load customer." However, TPPA is concerned that this approach may be
discriminatory, as the costs of building a facility would be allocated to a single customer even though the
facility will ultimately be used by the entire system.

       TPPA supports the Commission's goal of ensuring that large load customers pay their fair share
of costs, but believes this issue is more appropriately addressed under Project No. 58484, which evaluates
transmission cost recovery. Through Project No. 58484, the Commission can develop a transmission cost
allocation methodology that ensures all customers pay a just and equitable share of system-wide costs,
including system upgrade costs.

 Reassignment of CIAC Payments to the First Mover

         TPPA strongly discourages the Commission from reassigning CIAC given the administrative
complexity, however if the Commission chooses to move forward with assigning system upgrade costs to
the interconnecting large load customer that caused the need for the upgrades, TPPA provides the
following comments on proposed 25.194(h)(9)(C) regarding the reallocation of costs back to the first
mover.

Entitv Responsible for Reallocation

         TPPA requests clarity regarding which entity is responsible for calculating, notifying, collecting,
and distributing the CIAC payments as proposed. TPPA believes that if the Commission proceeds with
this reallocation, that the process and refunds will be highly controversial and administratively complex.
To that end, TPPA asserts that this responsibility should not fall to the interconnecting electric utility or
retail service provider, as they already have numerous responsibilities related to maintaining system
reliability, interconnecting new load and generation, and providing service to their customers.

         If the Commission proceeds with the drafted process, TPPA recommends that the Commission
itselfbe the entity responsible for calculating the costs to be reassigned, notifying the large load customers
of the reassignment, and collecting and redistributing the funds.

         If, instead, the Commission proposes that the interconnecting electric utility or the retail service
provider assume these responsibilities, TPPA requests that the rule codify the full process, including:

         •   A formula for calculating the costs to be reassigned;2
         •   The method for notification and associated timelines for responding and remitting payment;
         •   The type of payment acceptable to the interconnecting electric utility or retail service provider;
             and
         •   The method for remitting payments to the appropriate parties.

Applicabilitv to Other Customers

       TPPA notes that the proposed rule does not recognize that generation facilities and loads not
classified as large loads customers under this rule may also interconnect to the new facilities. TPPA
understands that these non-large load customers would not be required to pay CIAC payments to the
original large load customer under this proposal; only new large load customers would be subject to such

Timing Limitations

       Finally, TPPA recommends that the rule clearly state that this provision applies only to facilities
built after the adoption of the rule, and that the reallocation process ceases for facilities that have been
energized for more than five years.



Forms of Payment for CUC

       Proposed §25.194(h)(9)(D) provides that a large load may remit CIAC payments to an electric
utility in the form of cash, a corporate or parental guaranty, or a letter of credit. While TPPA does not at
this time object to these instruments being acceptable forms of payment for security deposits, TPPA
recognizes that both guaranties and letters of credit are impractical for CIAC payments. CIAC funds are
intended to be applied directly and expeditiously to the construction of interconnection facilities.
Requiring an electric utility to draw upon a letter of credit or pursue payment under a guaranty would

 introduce administrative delays and could hinder timely construction. Accordingly, TPPA recommends
that cash be the sole acceptable form of payment for CIAC obligations.



Refunding Financial Security

       As TPPA reads proposed 25.194(k)(1), the interconnecting utility is required to refund 20% ofthe
remaining security when the large load customer energizes. Additional security refunds are provided as
the large load customer meets milestones on its ramp schedule, proportional to the amount of load yet to
be energized to reach its contracted peak demand. However, proposed 25.194(k)(2) provides that any
remaining security balance must be refunded once the large load customer has sustained operations at its
contracted peak demand for five years. TPPA notes that there is a direct conflict between 25.194(k)(1)
and 25.194(k)(2), because under (k)(1) the total security will already have been refunded once the large
load reaches its contracted peak demand, leaving no security to be refunded under (k)(2).

       TPPA supports the concept in 25.194(k)(2), whereby the large load customer only receives a
complete refund of its security if it sustains operations at its contracted peak demand for a specified period,
and recommends extending that period to 10 years. To ensure security remains available for distribution
after this period, TPPA recommends refining 25.194(k)(1) so that only 50% of the remaining security is
returned ratably as the large load meets its ramp schedule milestones.

       Additionally, as noted above, TPPA seeks clarification that the security refund contemplated under
subsection (k) applies to security provided under both proposed subsections (e)(8) and (h)(8), and that the
security provided under subsection (h)(8) is not intended to cover an electric utility's costs for procuring
equipment and services to facilitate the interconnection, as those costs are addressed through and paid
under the CIAC.



Additional Standards Established by MOUs and Electric Cooperatives

       PURA § 37.0561(1) provides, "The commission may not limit the authority ofa municipally owned
utility or an electric cooperative to impose electric service requirements for large load customers on their
systems in addition to the standards adopted under this section." The proposed rule does not appear to
contemplate that a MOU or electric cooperative may develop additional standards necessary for their
system. TPPA recommends that the exact language of PURA § 37.0561(1) be added as a new subsection
in the rule to ensure consistency and maintain conformity between the Commission rule and PURA.

                 Texas Public Power Association's (TPPA) Executive Summary

TPPA recommends that an interconnecting electric utility not be held responsible for information
large load customers fail to provide.
TPPA recommends that the following items be explicitly deemed not competitively sensitive: the
name of the interconnecting electric utility; the contracted peak demand, or the requested peak
demand if the contracted peak demand is unknown; and the requested interconnection date.
TPPA recommends the rule recognize that the interconnecting electric utility will not always also be
the retail service provider.
TPPA requests that the rule clarify whether large load interconnection studies are to be conducted by
the interconnecting electric utility, ERCOT, or both. If the studies include ERCOT's analyses, TPPA
recommends that the rule provide additional information regarding the calculation of the study fee
for ERCOT's costs versus the interconnecting electric utility's costs.
TPPA recommends that the Commission provide clarification on when the interconnection
agreement should be issued and the information it should contain.
TPPA recommends that the discretionary service agreement, including the $50,000 per MW security,
be required before the interconnecting electric utility initiates any studies.
TPPA recommends large load customers be required to disclose plans for co-located generation and
backup generation that could export to the ERCOT grid or that would be unable to serve at least 50%
of the large load's requested or contracted peak demand.
TPPA recommends that the rule clarify whether additional studies requested by ERCOT will be
completed by the interconnecting electric utility or by ERCOT. If the additional studies are to be
completed by the interconnecting electric utility, TPPA objects to ERCOT determining the timeline
for completion of those studies.
TPPA supports the Commission requiring two securities-the $50,000 per MW security and an
amount aligned with the costs to interconnect the large load customer-to be held until after the
large load customer has completed and energized its interconnection. TPPA believes that the high
security requirements will ensure that large load customers pursue interconnection requests
intentionally and provide the market with certainty regarding realistic load interconnection requests.
TPPA recommends that the rule not specify that large load customers will fund system upgrade costs
incurred by the interconnecting electric utility to complete their interconnection.
TPPA strongly recommends the rule not require a CIAC reallocation from new large load customers
to original large load customers. However, if the Commission proceeds with this approach, TPPA
requests clarification on how CIAC payments will be calculated, who will calculate them, and the
processes for notification, collection, and distribution. TPPA asserts that this responsibility should
not fall on the interconnecting electric utility or retail service provider.
TPPA recommends that cash be the sole acceptable form of payment for CIAC obligations.
TPPA recommends that the rule extend the period during which the interconnecting electric utility
holds security from five years to ten years. Additionally, TPPA recommends refining § 25.194(k)(1)
so that only 50% of the remaining security is returned ratably as the large load customer meets its
ramp schedule milestones.
TPPA recommends that the exact language of PURA § 37.0561(1), regarding MOUs' and electric
cooperatives' authority to impose additional electric service requirements, be added as a new
subsection in the rule to ensure consistency and maintain conformity between the Commission rule
and PURA.
